query: For MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration materials, what single intervention could improve mechanical performance while retaining a large magnetocaloric effect? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected changes relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermomechanical treatment, involving an optimized annealing step followed by rapid quenching, will refine the grain structure and tailor dislocation density in MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration materials. This microstructural modification is expected to improve mechanical toughness (increased ductility and resistance to fatigue) while retaining the sharp magneto-structural transition that is responsible for a large magnetocaloric effect.
generation.material_initial_state: Pristine MnNiSi-based intermetallic materials possessing coarse grains, high brittleness, and a well-defined magneto-structural transition yielding a large magnetic entropy change.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermomechanical treatment protocol comprising an annealing step at a temperature near the magneto-structural transition followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be performed under conditions relevant to magnetic refrigeration: near the operational temperature range of the magneto-structural transition and under magnetic field strengths typical for cooling cycles. Processing must be optimized to avoid unwanted phase formation or excessive grain growth.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain refinement and a controlled dislocation network that improve stress distribution and inhibit crack propagation while preserving the integrity of the magneto-structural phase transition.
generation.mechanism: The thermomechanical treatment introduces a finer grain structure and an optimal density of dislocations, which distribute mechanical stress more evenly and arrest crack propagation, leading to increased ductility and toughness. At the same time, by avoiding compositional dilution or the formation of detrimental phases, the treatment preserves the abrupt magneto-structural transition needed for a large magnetocaloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated samples, the treated material will exhibit improved mechanical performance (e.g., enhanced tensile strength, ductility, and fracture toughness) while displaying a magnetocaloric effect (magnetic entropy change) that remains comparable, with any reduction kept within an acceptable margin (ideally less than 10-15%).
generation.baseline: Untreated MnNiSi-based materials with coarse-grained microstructures, which, despite exhibiting a large magnetocaloric effect, suffer from high brittleness and poor mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The benefits of the treatment are expected only when the processing parameters (annealing temperature, duration, and quenching rate) are carefully optimized. Deviations that lead to excessive grain growth or unwanted phase transformations may compromise both mechanical performance and the magnetocaloric properties.
generation.uncertainty: While the general trend of microstructural refinement improving mechanical properties is supported, the exact processing parameters and the precise tolerance of magnetocaloric effect reduction require empirical determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MnNiSi-based samples: one set will undergo the proposed thermomechanical treatment (optimized annealing followed by rapid quenching) and the other will remain untreated. Subject both sets to cyclic loading and magnetic field cycling within operational temperature ranges relevant to magnetic refrigeration.
measurements: Mechanical properties: tensile strength, ductility, fracture toughness, and fatigue resistance.
Magnetic properties: magnetic entropy change (ΔSm) measured at the critical magneto-structural transition under relevant field changes.
Microstructural analysis: grain size distribution and dislocation density via electron microscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in mechanical performance compared to untreated samples, or if the magnetocaloric effect (ΔSm) is reduced by more than approximately 10-15% relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The best way to decide the practicality of a material in magnetic cooling applications is by testing directly in a magnetic refrigerator, working on the principle of the AMRR (Active Magnetic Regenerative Refrigeration) cycle []. Recent investigations confirmed the magnetocaloric performance and the potential in magnetic refrigeration of the perovskite oxide Pr0.65Sr0.35MnO3 [,], which has the stoichiometry of our parent compound. When Ca substitutes for Sr in this compound, the magnetic parameters and magnetocaloric effect can be tuned for various temperature applications without significant changes in the magnitude of magnetic entropy change. Our investigations support the bulk polycrystalline Pr0.65Sr(0.35−x)CaxMnO3 compounds to be promising for magnetic cooling technology, while lower magnitude of magnetocaloric effect in nanocrystalline samples, unfortunately, seems to somewhat hinder their direct practical applications [,,].

The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. In the present study, we succeeded in tuning the microstructure and improving the room-temperature tensile properties of a high-performance Co-rich Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 (at%) TRIP-HEA, achieved by using thermomechanical processings of rolling and heat-treatment. The correlation between the microstructures and the strengthening mechanism of the samples at each stage was clarified. The grains were non-uniformly refined by the hot-rolling process but were significantly refined and homogenized after cold-rolling, followed by appropriate heat treatment. The grain size was refined from 144.4 μm to 1.83 μm by cold-rolling and subsequent annealing at 973 K; meanwhile, the Cr-rich σ-phase with a volume fraction of 0.413% and an average size of 118.8 nm was formed. It was found that grain refinement is the most effective method for enhancing the tensile strength while retaining ductility, whereas the formation of incoherent precipitates slightly improves strength but sacrifices ductility. frame.limitation: Current MnNiSi-based materials, while showing a robust magnetocaloric response, are limited by their mechanical fragility, which could hinder durability during cyclic loading and practical device integration.

decision.trend: Earlier research on functional magnetic alloys and high‐entropy materials has moved away from compositional dilution—such as alloying with secondary elements that may weaken the abruptness of the magneto‐structural transition—and toward processing-based methods that tailor the microstructure. For example, studies have used thermomechanical treatments to introduce refined grain sizes and controlled defect structures (such as ordered dislocations) in alloys, thereby improving mechanical properties like ductility and resistance to fatigue while preserving key functional transitions. The sequence of attempts started with altering alloy compositions and then evolved toward processing routes that create beneficial microstructures without compromising the key magnetocaloric behavior.
decision.unsolved: For MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration materials, it remains unresolved how to achieve the needed mechanical toughness (improved ductility and resistance to cyclic stresses) solely through microstructural engineering without interfering with the magnetostructural transformation responsible for the magnetocaloric effect.
decision.lever: Implementing a controlled thermomechanical treatment (for example, an optimized annealing protocol with rapid cooling) designed to induce grain refinement and a controlled dislocation density, thereby tailoring the microstructure to arrest crack propagation while preserving the sharp magneto-structural phase transition.
decision.why: This next step follows the trend seen in prior work where processing (rather than compositional changes) was used to enhance the mechanical performance of functional magnetic materials. For MnNiSi-based materials, a carefully tuned thermal or thermomechanical treatment can improve toughness by creating a fine-grained, defect-engineered microstructure without diluting the magnetic interactions that give rise to a large magnetocaloric effect.
